summary: The direct object — what is eaten, drunk, bought or liked — simply follows the verb: 我吃面包 ‘I eat bread’, 妈妈买鱼 ‘Mum buys fish’. Chinese has no cases: a noun looks the same as subject (面包在这里 ‘the bread is here’) and as object (我吃面包), and only its place after the verb makes it the object. So the order cannot change: 妈妈喜欢孩子 ‘the mother likes the child’, 孩子喜欢妈妈 ‘the child likes the mother’. A counted object keeps number + measure word: 我要一杯咖啡. Indirect objects (‘give him tea’) and objects with a preposition (‘with a friend’) come with the coverbs 给, 跟 in S11–S13 and in C03; other ways to place the object — as a topic (茶我不喝) or with 把 (我把茶喝了) — come much later.

items.title: The same noun as subject …
points: 面包在这里。 The bread is here.
茶是我的。 The tea is mine.

items.title: … and as object
points: 我吃面包。 I eat bread.

blocks.title: The position is the case
blocks.text: 妈妈喜欢孩子 ‘the mother likes the child’ — 孩子喜欢妈妈 ‘the child likes the mother’. Swap the nouns and you swap the roles. German can say Den Kaffee trinkt er because den shows the accusative; Chinese cannot move the object that way.

blocks.title: Verb + verb + object
blocks.text: 喜欢, 想 and 要 can take a second verb: 我喜欢喝茶 ‘I like drinking tea’, 我想吃鱼 ‘I’d like to eat fish’ — the object follows the last verb.

blocks.title: No preposition, no marker
blocks.text: 喜欢 takes its object directly: 我喜欢茶 (no ‘of’, no ‘von’). And 的 is not an object marker: ‘I eat bread’ is 我吃面包, not *我吃的面包.

blocks.title: What comes later
blocks.text: The indirect object (‘give the child milk’ — 给孩子牛奶) and objects with a preposition (跟, 给, 从 — ‘with’, ‘for’, ‘from’) come in S11–S13 and C03; the 把 construction (我把茶喝了 ‘I drank the tea up’) and the object as a topic (茶我不喝 ‘tea, I don’t drink’) much later.

askYourself: Who acts, and what is acted on? → the doer before the verb, the thing after it.
Is the object counted? → number + measure word before it: 我要两杯茶.
Is there a second verb (喜欢, 想, 要 + verb)? → the object follows the last verb: 我想喝水.
Did I mark the object somehow? → don’t: no ending, no particle, no 的.
steps: object (with number + measure word if counted)

traps: *我面包吃 → 我吃面包 (the object follows the verb).
*我吃的面包 for ‘I eat bread’ → 我吃面包.
German Den Tee trinke ich cannot be copied word for word: *茶喝我 would mean ‘the tea drinks me’.
*我要咖啡一杯 → 我要一杯咖啡 (number + measure word before the noun).

options: The mother and the child like each other.
quiz.why: The noun after the verb is the object.
Number + measure word + noun, after the verb.

quiz.q: How does Chinese mark the direct object?
options: by its place after the verb
with an ending, like German den / einen
quiz.answer: by its place after the verb
quiz.why: There are no cases in Chinese.

seeAlso.note: German marks the object with the accusative (den Kaffee, einen Apfel) and can move it to the front; Chinese marks it only by its place after the verb.
Arabic gives the object the ending -a / -an (أَكَلَ الْوَلَدُ تُفَّاحَةً ‘the boy ate an apple’); Chinese has no endings at all.
Hebrew puts אֶת before a definite object (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל אֶת הַלֶּחֶם); Chinese has no object marker — 我吃面包.
